# Bayesian inference and MCMC

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## From point estimates to posterior distributions

### Point estimation: least squares and maximum likelihood

- One [best]{style="color: tomato;"} value for each parameter, $\hat{\theta}$
- Uncertainty came afterwards, from standard errors or the profile likelihood

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The Bayesian formulation

So far we have asked *which* $\theta$ fits best. A Bayesian asks

[**"How plausible is each value of** $\theta$, given the data?"]{style="color: tomato;"}

- The answer is a [probability distribution]{style="color: tomato;"} over $\theta$
- Every estimate, interval and prediction we report comes from that one distribution

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bayesian inference is reallocation of credibility {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Before we see any data, each possible value of $\theta$ has some [prior]{style="color: tomato;"} credibility
- The data then make some values more believable and others less
- Bayes' rule is the rule for moving credibility towards the values that explain the data well

*Bayesian analysis is reallocation of credibility across possibilities. The rest is details.*
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/06_bayes_update.png)
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bayes' rule

$$p(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(y)}$$

- $p(\theta)$ is the [prior]{style="color: tomato;"}, what we believed before seeing the data $y$
- $p(y \mid \theta)$ is the [likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}, the same function we maximised in the MLE section
- $p(\theta \mid y)$ is the [posterior]{style="color: tomato;"}, what we believe now
- $p(y)$ is a normalising constant. It is the same number for every $\theta$, so it does not change the shape of the posterior

$$\text{posterior} \propto \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The prior

### Sources of prior information

- Earlier outbreaks and the literature, for example the infectious period of influenza
- Things we know must hold: rates are positive, proportions lie between 0 and 1
- What the people who know the disease think

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Vague and informative priors

- A [vague]{style="color: tomato;"} prior spreads credibility widely and leaves the work to the data
- An [informative]{style="color: tomato;"} prior writes down what we already know. It matters most when the data are thin
- Either way the prior is part of the model, so [say what it is, and check what it implies]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Prior predictive checks

:::::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Nobody has intuition for a prior on $\beta$. Everybody has intuition for an epidemic curve
- So draw parameter values from the prior, run the model, and look at the epidemics it produces
- If half of them put the whole school in bed by day two, the prior is telling you something you did not intend
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/06_flu_prior_predictive.png)
:::
:::::
::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The posterior

### Posterior summaries

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- A point estimate, if you want one: the posterior mean or median
- A [95% credible interval]{style="color: tomato;"}, the range that holds 95% of the posterior probability
- You can read it literally: *"there is a 95% probability that* $R_0$ lies between 3.4 and 3.7". A confidence interval does not allow that sentence
- Anything you can compute from the parameters, such as $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$, comes with its own distribution at no extra cost
- Predictions that carry the parameter uncertainty through
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The posterior is intractable

### The normalising constant

$$p(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta$$

- This is an integral over every combination of parameter values, and for an ODE model there is no formula for it
- What we *can* do is evaluate $p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$ at any $\theta$ we like, which gives us the posterior [up to that unknown constant]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Grid evaluation does not scale

| Parameters | Grid points at 15 values each |
|-----------:|------------------------------:|
|          2 |                           225 |
|          4 |                        50,625 |
|          6 |                    11,390,625 |
|         10 |               576,650,390,625 |

- With two parameters a grid is a fine way to *look at* the posterior
- With six it is out of the question

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Grid evaluation for the influenza outbreak

![](figures/06_flu_grid_posterior.png)

3,600 model runs, and nearly all of them landed where the posterior is zero

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Monte Carlo estimation {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
- If you want the mean height of the people of Kumasi you do not measure everyone. You measure a sample
- A posterior can be treated the same way. Given enough draws of $\theta$, the mean, the quantiles and the histogram of the sample are as good as the real thing
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/06_monte_carlo.png)
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Sampling from an unnormalised density

- Monte Carlo needs [samples]{style="color: tomato;"} from the posterior
- All we can do is [evaluate]{style="color: tomato;"} the posterior, up to a constant, at any point we choose

[**How do you draw samples from something you can only evaluate?**]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Markov chain Monte Carlo {.smaller}

[**Core idea:**]{style="color: tomato;"} generate the samples one after another as a [chain]{style="color: tomato;"}, where each new value depends only on the one before it (that is what *Markov* means), and set up the rule for the next step so that the chain spends time in each region in proportion to the posterior density

- Start somewhere. Propose a small move. Accept or reject it depending on how the posterior changes. Repeat
- Run it long enough and the values in the chain are draws from the posterior, and we [never had to compute $p(y)$]{style="color: tomato;"}
- The original version is the [Metropolis algorithm]{style="color: tomato;"}, which is what we build next

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Metropolis algorithm {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
1.  Start at some $\theta^{(0)}$
2.  Propose $\theta^* = \theta + \varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon$ comes from a [symmetric]{style="color: tomato;"} proposal distribution such as $N(0, \sigma^2)$
3.  Compute $r = \dfrac{p(\theta^* \mid y)}{p(\theta \mid y)}$. The constant $p(y)$ appears top and bottom and cancels
4.  Draw $u \sim U(0, 1)$. If $u < r$ accept the move ($\theta \leftarrow \theta^*$); otherwise stay where you are
5.  Record $\theta$ and go back to step 2
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figures/06_metropolis_flowchart.png)
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The acceptance rule

![](figures/06_metropolis_step.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Consequences of the acceptance rule

- If the proposal has higher posterior density than where we are, we [always]{style="color: tomato;"} take it
- If it has lower density we take it [with probability $r$]{style="color: tomato;"}. The chain can walk downhill, which is why it explores the distribution instead of climbing to the top and staying there
- When a proposal is rejected the current value is [written down again]{style="color: tomato;"}. Those repeats are part of the sample, so do not throw them away
- Put together, the chain visits each region in proportion to its posterior density

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Detailed balance and the stationary distribution

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- The acceptance rule gives the chain [detailed balance]{style="color: tomato;"}: as much probability flows from $\theta$ to $\theta^*$ as flows back, so nothing piles up anywhere $$p(\theta \mid y)\, q(\theta^* \mid \theta)\, \alpha(\theta, \theta^*) = p(\theta^* \mid y)\, q(\theta \mid \theta^*)\, \alpha(\theta^*, \theta)$$
- $\alpha = \min(1, r)$ is the smallest correction that makes this hold
- The posterior is then the chain's [stationary distribution]{style="color: tomato;"}. Run it long enough and its values are posterior draws
- With an asymmetric proposal the ratio needs a correction. That is [Metropolis–Hastings]{style="color: tomato;"}: $$r = \frac{p(\theta^* \mid y)\, q(\theta \mid \theta^*)}{p(\theta \mid y)\, q(\theta^* \mid \theta)}$$
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Practical implementation

### Tuning the proposal

![](figures/06_proposal_tuning.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Proposal scale and acceptance rate

- Make the proposal too narrow and nearly every move is accepted, but each move is tiny and the chain crawls
- Make it too wide and nearly every move is rejected, so the chain sits still for long stretches
- For a random walk proposal, aim for an acceptance rate of about [44% with one parameter, down to about 23% with many]{style="color: tomato;"}
- If the parameters are correlated in the posterior, the proposal should be correlated the same way

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Burn-in

![](figures/06_burn_in.png)

- We chose the starting point, so the first part of the chain says more about that choice than about the posterior
- Throw those early samples away. This is the [burn-in]{style="color: tomato;"}. Discarding a few extra costs little, and starting from a sensible place such as the MLE shortens it
- How much to discard is decided after looking at the chain, never before

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Convergence assessment with multiple chains

![](figures/06_convergence.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Convergence diagnostics

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- A single chain cannot tell you about the places it has never been
- So start several chains far apart. If they end up indistinguishable, they have found the same distribution
- [$\hat{R}$]{style="color: tomato;"} turns that into a number by comparing the variance between chains with the variance within them. We want $\hat{R}$ below 1.01
- Consecutive draws are correlated, so 20,000 of them carry less information than 20,000 independent draws would. The [effective sample size]{style="color: tomato;"} is the number that matters

``` {.r include="scripts/06_mcmc_schematics.R" snippet="rhat"}
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Convergence checklist

- The trace plots show no trend, the same spread at the start as at the end, and the chains lie on top of each other
- The acceptance rate is in a sensible range
- $\hat{R}$ is close to 1 and the effective sample size is in the hundreds at least
- [Any of these checks can show you a problem. None of them can prove there is not one]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Beyond the Metropolis algorithm {.smaller}

- [Metropolis-within-Gibbs]{style="color: tomato;"} updates one parameter, or one block of parameters, at a time, which helps when the parameters are correlated
- [Adaptive MCMC]{style="color: tomato;"} learns the proposal covariance from the chain while it runs, so you do not have to tune it by hand
- [Hamiltonian Monte Carlo]{style="color: tomato;"}, and its self-tuning version NUTS, uses the gradient of the log posterior to propose long moves in a sensible direction. It is the default sampler in Stan
- [Particle MCMC]{style="color: tomato;"} is for stochastic models, where the likelihood itself has to be estimated by simulation. That is the next section

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probabilistic programming languages

- You write down the model, the prior and the likelihood. The software does the sampling and reports the diagnostics
- Stan (through `rstan` or `cmdstanr`), `nimble`, `brms`, PyMC and Turing.jl all work this way

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Bayesian workflow

1.  Write down the model and the prior, and check the prior by simulating from it
2.  Write down the likelihood, that is, how the data arise from the model
3.  Sample the posterior with MCMC, using several chains started far apart
4.  Check the chains: trace plots, acceptance rate, $\hat{R}$, effective sample size
5.  Summarise the posterior: means, credible intervals, and derived quantities such as $R_0$
6.  Check the fit by plotting posterior predictions against the data

------------------------------------------------------------------------
